questions.title: Post-Partum Hemorrhage
questions.stem: With ongoing post-partum hemorrhage, what blood loss volume prompts consideration of immediate blood transfusion under 6.06?
questions.explanation: 6.06 ties immediate transfusion to ongoing hemorrhage with blood loss of 1,500 mL or more, or to any woman with tachycardia and hypotension — the vital-sign trigger matters because measured loss is almost always underestimated.

questions.title: Post-Partum Hemorrhage
questions.stem: Palpation of the fundus in a post-partum hemorrhage patient finds the uterus boggy rather than firm. What does 6.06 identify as the most likely etiology of the bleeding?
questions.explanation: 6.06 directs the crew to palpate the fundus for firmness or bogginess and its relation to the umbilicus; a boggy uterus makes atony the most likely source, which is why fundal massage and oxytocin follow immediately.

questions.title: Post-Partum Hemorrhage
questions.stem: After the placenta has been delivered, how much oxytocin does 6.06 direct be added to 1000 mL of NS/LR?
questions.explanation: Oxytocin 40 units goes into 1000 mL of NS/LR, infused up to 500 mL over 10 minutes and then at 50 mL/hr. The 10-unit figure is the IM dose used only when no IV is available.

questions.title: Post-Partum Hemorrhage
questions.stem: After the initial oxytocin infusion of up to 500 mL over 10 minutes, at what rate does 6.06 direct it be continued?
questions.explanation: The front-loaded 500 mL over 10 minutes gets uterine tone back; the infusion then drops to 50 mL/hr to maintain it without volume-loading an already compromised patient.

questions.title: Post-Partum Hemorrhage
questions.stem: Why does 6.06 warn against ever injecting undiluted oxytocin intravenously?
questions.explanation: Undiluted IV oxytocin can drop maternal blood pressure sharply in a patient who is already hemorrhaging. If no IV is available, 6.06 directs 10 units IM instead.

questions.title: Post-Partum Hemorrhage
questions.stem: What is the adult dose of methylergonovine for post-partum hemorrhage when oxytocin fails to produce adequate uterine contraction?
questions.explanation: Methylergonovine is the second-line uterotonic at 0.2 mg IM every 2 to 4 hours, used when oxytocin has not produced adequate contraction; 6.06 also suggests consulting the receiving physician or on-line medical control.

questions.title: Post-Partum Hemorrhage
questions.stem: Which finding does 6.06 give as a reason not to administer methylergonovine?
questions.explanation: Methylergonovine is a vasoconstrictor and should not be given when the SBP is above 140, since it can push an already hypertensive post-partum patient higher.

questions.title: Post-Partum Hemorrhage
questions.stem: In post-partum hemorrhage where the placenta has NOT yet been delivered, what does 6.06 direct the crew to do?
options: Begin fundal massage and start oxytocin at once
Provide gentle traction on the umbilical cord
Apply direct pressure to the perineum
questions.explanation: Gentle cord traction encourages delivery of the placenta; oxytocin and fundal massage are started only after it delivers, and the bladder is emptied first so the uterus can contract down.

questions.title: Post-Partum Hemorrhage
questions.stem: What does the BLS band of 6.06 direct a crew to do about the possible source of post-partum bleeding?
options: Provide gentle traction on the umbilical cord
Examine the perineum for lacerations and apply pressure
Palpate the fundus and begin fundal massage
questions.explanation: At BLS the treatment is via the Hypovolemic and Hemorrhagic Shock guideline plus a search for a laceration — perineal inspection and direct pressure. Fundal assessment and uterotonics sit in the CCT band.

questions.title: Pre-Eclampsia, Eclampsia, and Pregnancy Induced Hypertension
questions.stem: What is the magnesium sulfate loading dose for pre-eclampsia or eclampsia under 6.07?
questions.explanation: The load is 6 grams over 30 minutes, followed by a maintenance infusion. The 2-gram figure is the additional bolus for a breakthrough seizure, and 10 grams is the amount mixed into 250 mL to cover the load plus two hours of infusion.

questions.title: Pre-Eclampsia, Eclampsia, and Pregnancy Induced Hypertension
questions.stem: After the magnesium sulfate load in 6.07, at what rate is the maintenance infusion run?
questions.explanation: Maintenance is 2 grams/hr. The 1 gram/hr figure is the amount the infusion is increased by if a seizure occurs or persists despite the initial regimen.

questions.title: Pre-Eclampsia, Eclampsia, and Pregnancy Induced Hypertension
questions.stem: If the patient is actively seizing when magnesium sulfate is started under 6.07, over what period is the loading dose given?
questions.explanation: An actively seizing patient gets the load compressed to 15 minutes rather than 30, and the crew then moves to the seizure management section of the guideline.

questions.title: Pre-Eclampsia, Eclampsia, and Pregnancy Induced Hypertension
questions.stem: At what respiratory rate does 6.07 direct that magnesium sulfate be discontinued?
questions.explanation: Magnesium is stopped at a respiratory rate below 12 or when DTRs are absent. A rate below 8, or new cardiac arrhythmias, means frank magnesium toxicity and calls for calcium gluconate.

questions.title: Pre-Eclampsia, Eclampsia, and Pregnancy Induced Hypertension
questions.stem: A patient on a magnesium sulfate infusion develops a respiratory rate of 7 and new cardiac arrhythmias. What does 6.07 direct the crew to suspect?
questions.explanation: A respiratory rate under 8 or new arrhythmias on magnesium is toxicity until proven otherwise; the guideline directs discontinuing the magnesium and giving calcium gluconate.

questions.title: Pre-Eclampsia, Eclampsia, and Pregnancy Induced Hypertension
questions.stem: What is the calcium gluconate dose for suspected magnesium toxicity under 6.07?
options: 2 grams of 10% solution IV over 3 – 5 min
1 gram of 10% solution IV over 5 – 10 min
1 gram of 10% solution IM over 3 – 5 min
1 gram of 10% solution IV over 3 – 5 min
questions.explanation: A single 1-gram dose of 10% calcium gluconate over 3 to 5 minutes is usually sufficient because most patients are only marginally over the toxicity threshold; it may be re-dosed PRN.

questions.title: Pre-Eclampsia, Eclampsia, and Pregnancy Induced Hypertension
questions.stem: What does 6.07 warn may happen if calcium gluconate is infused too rapidly?
questions.explanation: Rapid calcium administration can produce bradycardia and arrhythmias, which is why the 1-gram dose is pushed over 3 to 5 minutes rather than given quickly.

questions.title: Pre-Eclampsia, Eclampsia, and Pregnancy Induced Hypertension
questions.stem: Seizure activity occurs despite a running magnesium sulfate infusion. What additional magnesium bolus does 6.07 direct?
questions.explanation: Magnesium sulfate remains the drug of choice for eclamptic seizures, so a breakthrough seizure gets an additional 2-gram bolus over 2 minutes rather than a switch to another agent.

questions.title: Pre-Eclampsia, Eclampsia, and Pregnancy Induced Hypertension
questions.stem: Alongside the additional bolus for a breakthrough eclamptic seizure, how does 6.07 direct the magnesium sulfate infusion be changed?
questions.explanation: The infusion is increased by 1 gram/hr on top of the 2-gram bolus, so the maintenance level rises to prevent recurrence rather than merely aborting the current seizure.

questions.title: Pre-Eclampsia, Eclampsia, and Pregnancy Induced Hypertension
questions.stem: An eclamptic seizure persists more than 2 minutes despite magnesium sulfate. What does 6.07 direct the crew to consider?
options: Administering a benzodiazepine while infusing magnesium
Doubling the magnesium sulfate infusion rate
questions.explanation: Magnesium stays running, but a seizure lasting beyond 2 minutes gets a benzodiazepine per the Seizure guideline added on top of it.

questions.title: Pre-Eclampsia, Eclampsia, and Pregnancy Induced Hypertension
questions.stem: What blood pressure goals does 6.07 set when treating hypertension in pre-eclampsia?
questions.explanation: Treatment continues until both thresholds are met — SBP 140 to 150 and DBP 90 to 100. Overcorrecting is explicitly warned against, since it compromises uteroplacental perfusion and causes fetal distress.

questions.title: Pre-Eclampsia, Eclampsia, and Pregnancy Induced Hypertension
questions.stem: What is the initial labetalol dose for blood pressure control under 6.07?
questions.explanation: Labetalol starts at 20 mg IV over 2 minutes, doubling to 40 mg and then 80 mg at 10-minute intervals if thresholds remain exceeded. The 5 mg over 1 minute figure is hydralazine, the alternative agent.

questions.title: Pre-Eclampsia, Eclampsia, and Pregnancy Induced Hypertension
questions.stem: Blood pressure thresholds are still exceeded 10 minutes after labetalol 20 mg IV. What dose does 6.07 direct next?
questions.explanation: The labetalol ladder doubles each step at 10-minute intervals: 20 mg, then 40 mg, then 80 mg. The infusion at 1 to 2 mg/min is reserved for pressure still uncontrolled after the bolus sequence.

questions.title: Pre-Eclampsia, Eclampsia, and Pregnancy Induced Hypertension
questions.stem: What maximum does 6.07 place on the labetalol infusion used when blood pressure remains uncontrolled?
questions.explanation: The labetalol infusion runs at 1 to 2 mg/min with a ceiling of 300 mg in 24 hours, counting everything given.

questions.title: Pre-Eclampsia, Eclampsia, and Pregnancy Induced Hypertension
questions.stem: What is the initial hydralazine dose for blood pressure control under 6.07?
questions.explanation: Hydralazine is the alternative to labetalol, starting at 5 mg IV over 1 minute, then 5 to 10 mg every 20 minutes if thresholds remain exceeded.

questions.title: Pre-Eclampsia, Eclampsia, and Pregnancy Induced Hypertension
questions.stem: What is the maximum cumulative hydralazine dose under 6.07?
questions.explanation: Repeat doses of 5 to 10 mg every 20 minutes stop at a cumulative total of 20 mg; beyond that an infusion of 0.5 to 10 mg/hr may be considered.

questions.title: Pre-Eclampsia, Eclampsia, and Pregnancy Induced Hypertension
questions.stem: What total fluid goal does 6.07 set for a pre-eclamptic patient, counting LR/NS plus infusions?
questions.explanation: Pre-eclamptic patients are prone to pulmonary edema, so total fluids including drug infusions are capped at 100 mL/hr — a deliberate departure from usual resuscitation habits.

questions.title: Pre-Eclampsia, Eclampsia, and Pregnancy Induced Hypertension
questions.stem: A pre-eclamptic patient develops a worsening frontal headache, blurred vision and epigastric pain. What does 6.07 say these findings indicate?
options: CNS involvement and a worsening condition
questions.explanation: These are central nervous system signs of worsening pre-eclampsia, and the guideline specifically notes that epigastric pain frequently precedes seizures — so airway, suction and oxygen go to hand.

questions.title: Pre-Eclampsia, Eclampsia, and Pregnancy Induced Hypertension
questions.stem: Which finding does 6.07 give as a criterion for SEVERE pre-eclampsia rather than mild?
options: SBP > 160 or DBP > 110 on 2 occasions, 6 hours apart
Edema developing at or beyond 20 weeks gestation
BP > 140/90 with > 300 mg proteinuria in 24 hours
questions.explanation: Severe pre-eclampsia is defined by any of several findings, among them SBP above 160 or DBP above 110 on two occasions 6 hours apart. The 140/90 with 300 mg proteinuria figure is mild pre-eclampsia.

questions.title: Pre-Term Labor and Premature Rupture of Membranes
questions.stem: Before transporting an interfacility patient with active contractions, at what cervical dilation does 6.08 require consultation with the sending and receiving providers?
questions.explanation: Active contractions with more than 5 cm dilation, or 100% effacement, require a conversation before moving the patient, because delivery in an aircraft or ambulance is worse than delivery at the sending facility.

questions.title: Pre-Term Labor and Premature Rupture of Membranes
questions.stem: When delivery appears imminent during an interfacility pre-term labor transfer, what does 6.08 advise?
options: It is better to deliver in the aircraft
Delay only if the patient is under 32 weeks
It is better to deliver at the sending facility
questions.explanation: The guideline says it is generally better to deliver at the sending facility than in the aircraft or ambulance, while acknowledging that local resources, flight duration and risk to mother and baby all factor in.

questions.title: Pre-Term Labor and Premature Rupture of Membranes
questions.stem: With no guidance from the sending provider, what contraction pattern prompts tocolysis under 6.08?
options: Less than 10 minutes apart, lasting over 30 seconds
Less than 5 minutes apart, lasting over 60 seconds
Less than 15 minutes apart, lasting over 30 seconds
Any palpable contraction before 37 weeks gestation
questions.explanation: Contractions closer than 10 minutes apart that last longer than 30 seconds are the trigger for choosing one of the tocolytics, absent direction from the sending provider.

questions.title: Pre-Term Labor and Premature Rupture of Membranes
questions.stem: What is the magnesium sulfate loading dose and maintenance rate for pre-term labor under 6.08?
questions.explanation: Tocolysis with magnesium uses the same 6-gram load over 30 minutes and 2 grams/hour maintenance as the pre-eclampsia guideline; 10 grams in 250 mL supplies the load plus two hours of infusion.

questions.title: Pre-Term Labor and Premature Rupture of Membranes
questions.stem: For which pre-term labor patients is magnesium sulfate the first-line tocolytic under 6.08?
options: Under 32 weeks with delivery expected within 24 hours
Over 32 weeks gestation with an SBP below 90
Patients in whom nifedipine is contraindicated
Under 37 weeks with any palpable contractions
questions.explanation: Magnesium is chosen first for patients under 32 weeks gestation when delivery is expected within 24 hours; nifedipine is first line for everyone else, and terbutaline only when both are contraindicated.

questions.title: Pre-Term Labor and Premature Rupture of Membranes
questions.stem: What is the nifedipine dose, route and interval for tocolysis under 6.08?
questions.explanation: Nifedipine 10 mg sublingual or oral every 15 minutes is first line for patients who do not meet the magnesium criteria; 40 mg is the total ceiling, not a single dose.

questions.title: Pre-Term Labor and Premature Rupture of Membranes
questions.stem: What is the maximum total nifedipine dose for tocolysis under 6.08?
questions.explanation: Repeat 10 mg doses every 15 minutes stop once a total of 40 mg has been given.

questions.title: Pre-Term Labor and Premature Rupture of Membranes
questions.stem: At what blood pressure does 6.08 direct nifedipine be held?
questions.explanation: Nifedipine is a vasodilator, so it is held for an SBP below 90. The same hypotension risk is why nifedipine and magnesium are used together only on a provider's order.

questions.title: Pre-Term Labor and Premature Rupture of Membranes
questions.stem: What is the terbutaline dose, route and interval for tocolysis under 6.08?
questions.explanation: Terbutaline 0.25 mg subcutaneously every 30 minutes is repeated until tocolysis is achieved, and is reserved for when nifedipine and magnesium are both contraindicated.

questions.title: Pre-Term Labor and Premature Rupture of Membranes
questions.stem: At what heart rate does 6.08 direct terbutaline be held?
questions.explanation: Terbutaline is a beta agonist and reliably produces maternal tachycardia, so it is held once the heart rate exceeds 120.

questions.title: Pre-Term Labor and Premature Rupture of Membranes
questions.stem: When does 6.08 direct terbutaline be used for tocolysis?
options: When the patient's systolic pressure is below 90
As first line when delivery is expected within 24 hours
As first line for patients under 32 weeks gestation
When nifedipine and magnesium are contraindicated
questions.explanation: Terbutaline sits third in the tocolytic order, used only when both nifedipine and magnesium sulfate are contraindicated.

questions.title: Pre-Term Labor and Premature Rupture of Membranes
questions.stem: Which of the following does 6.08 list as a contraindication to tocolysis?
questions.explanation: Chorioamnionitis is one of the listed contraindications, along with gestational age under 20 weeks, maternal cardiac disease, vaginal bleeding or suspected abruption, fetal demise, and evidence of fetal compromise.

questions.title: Pre-Term Labor and Premature Rupture of Membranes
questions.stem: After premature rupture of membranes, what fetal heart rate prompts consideration of chorioamnionitis under 6.08?
questions.explanation: Maternal fever or fetal tachycardia above 160 bpm raises chorioamnionitis and other sources of infection, which is one of the triggers for discussing antibiotics with the sending and receiving providers before transfer.

questions.title: Pre-Term Labor and Premature Rupture of Membranes
questions.stem: Why does 6.08 restrict concurrent use of nifedipine and magnesium sulfate to an order from the sending provider, receiving provider or OLMC?
questions.explanation: Both agents drop maternal blood pressure, so stacking them without an order risks hypotension in a patient whose uteroplacental perfusion is already the concern.

questions.title: Trauma in Pregnancy
questions.stem: What does 6.09 Trauma in Pregnancy identify as the highest priority in managing an injured pregnant patient?
questions.explanation: Maternal resuscitation comes first because fetal survival depends on maternal perfusion and oxygenation; everything else in the guideline is secondary to that.

questions.title: Trauma in Pregnancy
questions.stem: What does 6.09 give as the initial treatment for hypotension in a pregnant trauma patient?
options: Trendelenburg positioning with the legs elevated
Left lateral tilt by placing a wedge under the right hip
Immediate vasopressor infusion for uterine perfusion
A rapid crystalloid bolus before any repositioning
questions.explanation: Relieving aortocaval compression comes first — a wedge under the right hip, or tipping the backboard if the patient is immobilized — before fluids or anything else.

questions.title: Trauma in Pregnancy
questions.stem: A pregnant trauma patient has a rigid, painful abdomen and no vaginal bleeding. What does 6.09 say this presentation often represents?
questions.explanation: 6.09 directs crews to distinguish abdominal pain from contractions and notes that abruption often presents as a rigid, painful abdomen — with vaginal bleeding that may or may not be present.

questions.title: Trauma in Pregnancy
questions.stem: Why does 6.09 emphasise assessment for chest injury in a pregnant trauma patient?
options: Chest injury is a common cause of placental abruption
The elevated diaphragm raises the risk of hypoventilation
Pulmonary edema develops earlier in pregnant patients
Rib fractures are far more common during pregnancy
questions.explanation: The gravid uterus elevates the diaphragm, increasing the risk of atelectasis and hypoventilation; any resulting hypoxia shunts blood away from the uterus and harms the fetus.

questions.title: Trauma in Pregnancy
questions.stem: Who does 6.09 direct should perform the pelvic examination for cervical dilation and effacement on an interfacility pregnant trauma patient?
questions.explanation: The sending facility performs the exam where possible, as part of assessing for pre-term labor that may follow trauma; LFN clinicians do not perform digital pelvic exams.

questions.title: Trauma in Pregnancy
questions.stem: What does 6.09 say about vasopressor use in a hypotensive pregnant trauma patient?
options: They are a last resort, as they reduce uterine blood flow
They are first line once 1000 mL of crystalloid is given
They are preferred over blood to avoid fluid overload
They are absolutely contraindicated at any point in pregnancy
questions.explanation: Vasopressors constrict uterine vessels and worsen fetal hypoxia, so persistent hypotension and shock are treated with fluids and blood per the Hypovolemic and Hemorrhagic Shock guideline first.

questions.title: Trauma in Pregnancy
questions.stem: When transferring a pregnant trauma patient from another facility, what fetal monitor finding does 6.09 direct the crew to note specifically?
options: A fetal heart rate above 160 bpm
questions.explanation: The guideline directs reviewing the strip and obtaining a copy if available, with specific attention to late or variable decelerations as evidence of fetal compromise.

questions.title: Vaginal Bleeding
questions.stem: What oxygen saturation target does the BLS band of 6.10 set for a patient with vaginal bleeding?
questions.explanation: Supplemental oxygen is given to keep the SpO2 at or above 94%, maximising oxygen delivery to the fetus while maternal blood volume is falling.

questions.title: Vaginal Bleeding
questions.stem: How does 6.10 direct a BLS crew to perform uterine massage for active post-partum hemorrhage from the vagina?
options: From the pubis toward the umbilicus, clockwise
In small circles centred on the umbilicus
From the umbilicus toward the pubis, clockwise
From the pubis toward the umbilicus, anticlockwise
questions.explanation: Firm massage runs from the pubis up toward the umbilicus in a clockwise direction; the aim is to make the boggy uterus contract down on the bleeding placental bed.

questions.title: Vaginal Bleeding
questions.stem: What does 6.10 note about maternal vital signs during ongoing obstetric hemorrhage?
options: They typically do not change until blood loss is significant
They change sooner than in a non-pregnant trauma patient
Hypotension consistently appears before any tachycardia
Tachycardia is reliably the earliest and most sensitive sign
questions.explanation: Pregnancy expands maternal blood volume, so vital signs stay deceptively normal until a large volume has been lost — normal numbers do not mean the patient is stable.

questions.title: Vaginal Bleeding
questions.stem: Which tocolytic does 6.10 identify as contraindicated in a patient with vaginal bleeding?
questions.explanation: Terbutaline is contraindicated outright; magnesium tocolysis is possible but only after consultation with the sending and/or receiving provider, and no tocolytic is given to an actively bleeding patient.

questions.title: Vaginal Bleeding
questions.stem: With which condition does 6.10 identify speculum and digital pelvic exams as contraindicated?
questions.explanation: Instrumenting the vagina in previa can provoke catastrophic hemorrhage. LFN personnel do not perform these exams, but crews must recognise the contraindication when a sending facility proposes one.

questions.title: Vaginal Bleeding
questions.stem: For excessive vaginal bleeding with hypotension and/or tachycardia, what does the CCT band of 6.10 direct?
questions.explanation: Hypotension or tachycardia with heavy bleeding is the CCT trigger for blood products, in keeping with the 1500 mL figure used elsewhere in the obstetric guidelines.

questions.title: Vaginal Bleeding
questions.stem: What does 6.10 describe as the classic presentation of placenta previa?
options: A rigid, painful abdomen with marked uterine tenderness
Painless bleeding with fetal distress and early coagulopathy
Abdominal and back pain with no vaginal bleeding at all
Painless vaginal bleeding in the second or third trimester
questions.explanation: Previa classically bleeds painlessly, with a soft uterus, usually no fetal distress and less coagulopathy; contractions may or may not be present.

questions.title: Vaginal Bleeding
questions.stem: How does 6.10 define abruptio placentae?
options: Separation of the placenta during the third stage of labor
Implantation of the placenta over the internal cervical os
Failure of the placenta to deliver within 30 minutes of birth
Premature separation of the placenta after the 20th week
questions.explanation: Abruption is premature separation after the 20th week and before birth; it is a clinical diagnosis from abdominal or back pain, uterine tenderness, contractions and fetal distress, and may produce no visible bleeding at all.

questions.title: Burns and Inhalation Injuries
questions.stem: A burn patient has carbonaceous sputum and singed nasal hairs but an SpO2 of 99%. What oxygen does 7.01 direct?
options: 100% oxygen by maximum flow non-rebreather mask
Oxygen titrated to maintain an SpO2 of at least 94%
Oxygen by nasal cannula at 6 litres per minute
No oxygen unless the saturation falls below 90%
questions.explanation: Signs of inhalation injury get 100% oxygen at maximum flow regardless of the pulse oximeter, because carboxyhemoglobin reads as saturated — 7.01 says explicitly not to base oxygen need on SpO2 values.

questions.title: Burns and Inhalation Injuries
questions.stem: What dressing does 7.01 direct a crew to place over a burn?
options: Wet-to-dry gauze over the burned surface
Moist saline dressings for any size burn
Moist dressings for burns under 10% TBSA
questions.explanation: Burns are covered with dry, clean or sterile linen and the patient monitored for hypothermia; 7.01 states that moist dressings are no longer recommended for any size burn.

questions.title: Burns and Inhalation Injuries
questions.stem: How does 7.01 direct a crew to transport a patient with severe upper body burns?
options: In a left lateral tilt position
Supine with the head of the bed flat
questions.explanation: Upright positioning limits dependent swelling of the face and neck in upper body burns, buying time before airway edema closes off the airway.

questions.title: Burns and Inhalation Injuries
questions.stem: What is the adult pre-hospital fluid resuscitation rate for burns under 7.01?
questions.explanation: Adults get lactated ringers at 500 mL/hr through a fluid warmer where possible, with normal saline used only if LR is unavailable. On interfacility transfers the crew may instead continue the rate the sending facility set.

questions.title: Burns and Inhalation Injuries
questions.stem: What pre-hospital burn fluid rate does 7.01 set for a child aged 6 to 12 years?
questions.explanation: Children 6 to 12 get 250 mL/hr; the 125 mL/hr rate applies to children 5 and under and 500 mL/hr is the adult rate. Lactated ringers is preferred but NS may be used.

questions.title: Burns and Inhalation Injuries
questions.stem: What pre-hospital burn fluid rate does 7.01 set for a child aged 5 years or younger?
questions.explanation: Children 5 and under get 125 mL/hr — half the rate used for 6 to 12 year olds — reflecting their smaller circulating volume.

questions.title: Burns and Inhalation Injuries
questions.stem: In addition to the burn resuscitation fluid, what does 7.01 direct for a pediatric burn patient weighing under 30 kg?
questions.explanation: Small children deplete glycogen quickly, so those under 30 kg also receive D5LR at maintenance rate per the Basic Approach guideline, with D5NS substituted if D5LR is unavailable.

questions.title: Burns and Inhalation Injuries
questions.stem: At what rate does 7.01 start norepinephrine in a pediatric burn patient still hypotensive after adequate fluid resuscitation?
questions.explanation: Vasopressors come only after adequate volume in burns, because the underlying problem is plasma loss. The pediatric start is 0.05 mcg/kg/min, titrated every 3 to 5 minutes.

questions.title: Burns and Inhalation Injuries
questions.stem: Norepinephrine is titrated every 3 to 5 minutes in 7.01 to what maximum rate?
questions.explanation: The ceiling is 45 mcg/min for both adults and children. The PEARLS note that this maximum may be exceeded if the patient stays hypotensive despite adequate fluid and a second vasopressor.

questions.title: Burns and Inhalation Injuries
questions.stem: For which burn transports does 7.01 direct insertion of a urinary catheter?
options: Any transport of a patient with over 20% TBSA
questions.explanation: Urine output is the practical measure of burn resuscitation, so a catheter goes in for interfacility transports over 30 minutes, with output monitored and documented every 30 minutes.

questions.title: Burns and Inhalation Injuries
questions.stem: What is the adult target urine output for a burn patient under the CCT band of 7.01?
questions.explanation: Adults are resuscitated to 0.5 mL/kg/hr; 0.5 to 1 mL/kg/hr is the pediatric target, while the higher figures apply to electrical burns. Dark or red urine signals the need for more fluid, not less.

questions.title: Burns and Inhalation Injuries
questions.stem: Because of catecholamine release and hypermetabolism after a burn, what does 7.01 consider a normal adult heart rate?
questions.explanation: A burn patient at 110 is not necessarily under-resuscitated; 7.01 treats 100 to 120 as normal, and rates above that as a prompt to look for hypovolemia, hypoxemia or unrelieved pain.

questions.title: Burns and Inhalation Injuries
questions.stem: Which burns does 7.01 direct be excluded from the TBSA estimate?
questions.explanation: First degree burns are red and painful but do not leak plasma, so including them inflates the TBSA figure and over-resuscitates the patient.

questions.title: Burns and Inhalation Injuries
questions.stem: Under the Idaho burn trauma criteria in 7.01, what electrical injury voltage makes a patient Priority 1?
questions.explanation: High voltage electrical injury at or above 500V is Priority 1, alongside intubation, actual or potential airway compromise and suspected inhalation injury.

questions.title: Burns and Inhalation Injuries
questions.stem: In the consensus burn formula in 7.01, what volume multiplier is used for a patient aged 14 years or older?
options: 1 mL x weight in kg x TBSA
3 mL x weight in kg x TBSA
2 mL x weight in kg x TBSA
4 mL x weight in kg x TBSA
questions.explanation: The consensus formula spans 2 to 4 mL per kg per percent TBSA: 2 mL for age 14 and over, 3 mL under 14, and 4 mL for electrical burns.

questions.title: Burns and Inhalation Injuries
questions.stem: How does 7.01 direct the calculated burn resuscitation volume be distributed over time?
options: Half over the first 12 hours, the rest over the next 12
Half over the first 8 hours, the rest over the next 16
Half over the first 4 hours, the rest over the next 20
Evenly across the first 24 hours after the burn
questions.explanation: The clock starts at the time of the burn, not at crew arrival — half the calculated volume in the first 8 hours post burn and the second half across the following 16.

questions.title: Burns and Inhalation Injuries
questions.stem: To which facility does 7.01 direct burn patients in the Portland Metro area be transported?
questions.explanation: Outside Idaho, most burn patients go to the closest appropriate receiving facility unless on-line medical control directs otherwise, but Portland Metro patients go to Legacy Emanuel.

questions.title: Entrapment
questions.stem: What does the BLS band of 7.02 say about tourniquet use in an entrapped patient?
options: They should only be used to control active bleeding
They should be applied before extrication begins
They should be applied to any entrapped limb
They should be released every 20 minutes in transit
questions.explanation: Tourniquets are reserved for active bleeding in entrapment; prophylactic application adds ischemic load to a limb already at risk of crush injury.

questions.title: Entrapment
questions.stem: For a suspected pelvic crushing injury in an entrapped patient, what does 7.02 direct a BLS crew to consider?
questions.explanation: A pelvic binder limits the volume into which the pelvis can bleed, and it goes on before extrication rather than after the patient is moved.

questions.title: Entrapment
questions.stem: Which ECG changes does 7.02 direct a crew to treat as hyperkalemia in an entrapped crush patient?
options: A new left bundle branch block
Peaked T waves or a widened QRS complex
ST elevation in the inferior leads
questions.explanation: Crushed muscle releases potassium, and peaked T waves or QRS widening on the monitor are the cue to treat per the Hyperkalemia section of Electrolyte Disturbances — before the rhythm degenerates.

questions.title: Entrapment
questions.stem: For an adult with severe crush injury, what fluid does 7.02 direct before extrication?
options: NS/LR 500 mL, then an infusion at 250 mL/hr
NS/LR 1000-2000 mL, then an infusion at 500 mL/hr
NS/LR 20 mL/kg, then twice maintenance rate
questions.explanation: Volume loading before release dilutes the potassium and myoglobin washout that follows extrication, so 1000 to 2000 mL goes in first and an infusion at 500 mL/hr continues afterwards.

questions.title: Entrapment
questions.stem: What is the pediatric fluid regimen before extrication for severe crush injury under 7.02?
questions.explanation: Children get 10 to 20 mL/kg of NS/LR before extrication followed by a 5 mL/kg/hour infusion; the 20 to 40 mL/kg figure belongs to the CCT band.

questions.title: Entrapment
questions.stem: What is the calcium gluconate dose for suspected or present hyperkalemia under 7.02?
options: 1 gram of 10% solution slow IV over 5-10 minutes
50 mEq of 10% solution slow IV over 5 minutes
2 grams of 10% solution slow IV over 5 minutes
1 gram of 10% solution IV over 3 – 5 minutes
questions.explanation: Calcium stabilises the myocardium against hyperkalemia; 7.02 gives 1 gram of the 10% solution slowly over 5 to 10 minutes, and it must not share a line with sodium bicarbonate.

questions.title: Entrapment
questions.stem: What sodium bicarbonate dose does 7.02 direct for suspected or present hyperkalemia?
questions.explanation: Sodium bicarbonate 50 mEq IV shifts potassium intracellularly. Like calcium it must not be run through the same line as the other, as the two precipitate.

questions.title: Entrapment
questions.stem: What albuterol dose does 7.02 direct for suspected or present hyperkalemia?
questions.explanation: The hyperkalemia dose of albuterol is far higher than the bronchospasm dose — 10 mg nebulised — because the aim is beta-driven intracellular potassium shift, not bronchodilation.

questions.title: Entrapment
questions.stem: What line precaution does 7.02 specify when giving calcium gluconate and sodium bicarbonate for hyperkalemia?
options: They must not be given through the same IV line
Calcium must be given by intraosseous access only
They must be given through the same IV line
Both must be diluted in the same 250 mL bag
questions.explanation: Calcium and bicarbonate precipitate on contact, so each is given through its own line — a point 7.02 makes twice, once under each drug.

questions.title: Entrapment
questions.stem: What is the adult sodium bicarbonate infusion rate in the CCT band of 7.02?
questions.explanation: Adults get a sodium bicarbonate infusion at 250 mL/hr, mixed as 3 amps in 850 mL of D5W where available.

questions.title: Entrapment
questions.stem: What is the pediatric sodium bicarbonate infusion rate in the CCT band of 7.02?
questions.explanation: Children run at 5 mL/kg/hr capped at 250 mL/hr, so a large child never exceeds the adult rate.

questions.title: Entrapment
questions.stem: How does 7.02 direct the sodium bicarbonate infusion be mixed?
options: 3 amps in 1000 mL of normal saline
questions.explanation: Three amps go into 850 mL of D5W if available; if it is not, normal saline is infused at the same rate instead, but bicarbonate is never mixed into saline.

questions.title: Entrapment
questions.stem: What role does 7.02 describe for a venous tourniquet during extrication of a prolonged crush patient?
options: Preventing compartment syndrome in the trapped limb
Controlling the effects of hyperkalemia on release
Controlling arterial bleeding from a crushed limb
questions.explanation: A venous tourniquet can blunt the sudden systemic washout of potassium when a long-entrapped limb is freed, buying time for the hyperkalemia treatments to work.

questions.title: Extremity Trauma
questions.stem: Where does 7.03 direct a tourniquet be placed for extremity bleeding uncontrolled by other means?
options: At least 5 cm proximal to the injury, over bare skin
Directly over the wound, over bare skin
At least 5 cm distal to the injury, over clothing
At the most proximal point of the limb
questions.explanation: The tourniquet sits at least 5 cm proximal to the injury and directly on exposed skin, so clothing cannot pad the windlass and leave arterial flow intact.

questions.title: Extremity Trauma
questions.stem: Once a tourniquet has been applied under 7.03, what does the guideline direct?
options: Remove it once a pressure dressing is in place
Record the time applied; do not loosen without a physician order
Convert it to a pressure dressing before transport
Loosen it every 20 minutes to perfuse the limb
questions.explanation: The application time is recorded for the receiving team, and the tourniquet stays on — loosening or removing it requires a physician's order.

questions.title: Extremity Trauma
questions.stem: How does 7.03 direct a crew to prepare an amputated part for transport?
options: Submerge the part directly in a container of sterile saline
Wrap in dry sterile gauze and keep it at room temperature
Wrap in moist sterile saline dressing, bag it, cool in ice water
Pack the part directly in ice to preserve the tissue
questions.explanation: Gross debris and clothing come off, the part is wrapped in moist sterile saline dressing and sealed in a plastic bag, and the bag goes into ice water — direct tissue contact with ice causes freezing injury.

questions.title: Extremity Trauma
questions.stem: For an open fracture, what does 7.03 direct be applied over the wound before splinting, if time permits?
questions.explanation: Open fractures get a saline moistened dressing over the wound and then the splint; the dry dressing convention applies to other open wounds, not to exposed bone.

questions.title: Extremity Trauma
questions.stem: For which injury does 7.03 direct application of a traction splint when time permits?
options: A dislocated knee with vascular compromise
A suspected mid shaft or proximal femur fracture
An open tibia and fibula fracture
questions.explanation: Traction splints are for suspected mid shaft or proximal femur fractures, and may be used in the presence of a lower extremity fracture; Sager splints handle multilevel fractures with minimal traction.

questions.title: Extremity Trauma
questions.stem: When does 7.03 direct the neurovascular examination of an injured extremity be repeated?
options: Only on arrival at the receiving facility
questions.explanation: Function, sensation and vascular status are checked proximal and distal to the injury, and the examination is repeated after splinting — a splint is the commonest cause of a newly pulseless limb.

questions.title: Extremity Trauma
questions.stem: Within what time from injury does 7.03 require tranexamic acid be given?
questions.explanation: TXA is considered only for patients meeting blood administration criteria, when the time of injury is 2 hours or less, and after all other life threats have been addressed.

questions.title: Extremity Trauma
questions.stem: What is the adult tranexamic acid dose under 7.03?
options: 2 grams IV in 100 mL NS over 10 minutes
15 mg/kg IV in 100 mL NS over 10 minutes
1 gram IV in 100 mL NS over 10 minutes
2 grams IV push over 3 to 5 minutes
questions.explanation: Adults receive 2 grams in 100 mL of normal saline over 10 minutes, which is also the maximum. The 15 mg/kg figure is the pediatric dose.

questions.title: Extremity Trauma
questions.stem: What is the pediatric tranexamic acid dose and maximum under 7.03?
options: 30 mg/kg IV over 10 minutes; max 1 gram
2 grams IV over 10 minutes; max 2 grams
15 mg/kg IV over 10 minutes; max 1 gram
15 mg/kg IV over 10 minutes; max 2 grams
questions.explanation: Children get 15 mg/kg in 100 mL of NS over 10 minutes, capped at 1 gram — half the adult ceiling.

questions.title: Extremity Trauma
questions.stem: For an open fracture in a patient over 50 kg, what cefazolin dose does 7.03 direct?
questions.explanation: Cefazolin 2 grams by slow IV push over 3 to 5 minutes is the dose above 50 kg, and it is given only after all other care and stabilization is complete.

questions.title: Extremity Trauma
questions.stem: For an open fracture in a patient weighing 50 kg or less, what cefazolin dose does 7.03 direct?
questions.explanation: At or below 50 kg the dose is weight-based at 30 mg/kg by slow IV push over 3 to 5 minutes, capped at the 2-gram adult dose.

questions.title: Extremity Trauma
questions.stem: Under 7.03, when should a grossly angulated limb or major joint dislocation be realigned?
options: Only after arrival at the receiving facility
Whenever the limb is visibly deformed
Only if vascularly compromised or unable to load aboard
Only once procedural sedation has been given
questions.explanation: Realignment is reserved for restoring perfusion when there is vascular compromise from the fracture or dislocation, or when the limb cannot be loaded into the aircraft or vehicle; sedation and pain management are considered if time and hemodynamics allow.

questions.title: General Trauma Care
questions.stem: What oxygen delivery does 7.04 direct for most trauma patients during the rapid trauma assessment?
options: Oxygen only if the SpO2 falls below 94%
Nasal cannula at 2 litres per minute
questions.explanation: Airway assessment in 7.04 includes clearing the mouth and positioning, and the guideline states that most trauma patients should receive oxygen via an NRB mask.

questions.title: General Trauma Care
questions.stem: For which trauma patients does 7.04 direct application of a cervical collar and cervical immobilization device?
options: Only patients with a neurologic deficit
questions.explanation: Blunt trauma scene calls get a collar and immobilization device. Spinal immobilization is explicitly not required for penetrating trauma, where it delays care without benefit.

questions.title: General Trauma Care
questions.stem: How does 7.04 direct the pelvis be evaluated for instability during the secondary assessment?
options: Rock the pelvis in both directions
Compress the iliac crests once, from the side
Push down on the iliac crests twice
questions.explanation: The iliac crests are compressed only once and only from the side. Distracting the pelvis by pushing down increases the space into which it can bleed.

questions.title: General Trauma Care
questions.stem: Why does 7.04 forbid repeated or vigorous manipulation of the pelvis in a patient with pelvic fractures?
options: It reliably causes pain that will require sedation
It can injure the bladder and the urethra
Clots can be dislodged and increase blood loss
It makes a pelvic binder impossible to seat
questions.explanation: Clot already formed at fracture surfaces is the only thing limiting retroperitoneal bleeding, and repeated manipulation dislodges it.

questions.title: General Trauma Care
questions.stem: How does 7.04 direct eviscerated abdominal organs be covered?
options: With a sterile moist saline dressing
By replacing them and binding the abdomen
With an occlusive commercial chest seal
questions.explanation: Eviscerated organs get a sterile moist saline dressing to prevent drying, while other open abdominal wounds are covered with dry sterile dressing.

questions.title: General Trauma Care
questions.stem: What finding does 7.04 give as a reason not to place a urinary catheter on an interfacility trauma transport?
questions.explanation: Blood at the meatus suggests urethral disruption, and passing a catheter through it can convert a partial tear into a complete one.

questions.title: General Trauma Care
questions.stem: Which cluster of findings does 7.04 list as signs of tension pneumothorax prompting needle thoracostomy?
options: Hypoxia with diffuse wheezing and stridor
Hypotension with a rigid, distended abdomen
questions.explanation: 7.04 lists hypotension, hypoxia, JVD, hypocarbia and respiratory distress or failure as the tension picture. The hypertension-bradycardia-irregular respiration triad is Cushing reflex, a head injury sign.

questions.title: General Trauma Care
questions.stem: How does 7.04 direct an open pneumothorax be sealed?
options: With a dry sterile dressing held by direct pressure
With an occlusive dressing taped on all four sides
By immediate needle thoracostomy on the same side
With a commercial chest seal or a 3-sided dressing
questions.explanation: A commercial chest seal or a 3-sided dressing lets trapped air escape; a fully occlusive dressing converts an open pneumothorax into a tension pneumothorax.

questions.title: General Trauma Care
questions.stem: On which patients does 7.04 direct bilateral finger thoracostomies be performed?
options: All patients with a suspected tension pneumothorax
Only patients with absent breath sounds on one side
All traumatic arrest patients, with one stated exception
questions.explanation: Bilateral finger thoracostomies go on every traumatic arrest patient, except those already pulseless on EMS arrival whose resuscitation was terminated per the termination of resuscitation guideline.

questions.title: General Trauma Care
questions.stem: Under what conditions does 7.04 permit chest tube insertion?
options: Only on sending provider orders and in a sterile fashion
Only after needle decompression has been attempted twice
At the discretion of the transporting CCT crew
Whenever a finger thoracostomy has failed to decompress
questions.explanation: Chest tube insertion is the one chest decompression procedure in 7.04 that requires an order from the sending provider, and it is done only when sterility can be maintained.

questions.title: General Trauma Care
questions.stem: How does 7.04 direct epinephrine 1:100,000 be prepared for injection into a bleeding scalp wound?
options: Mix 1 mL of 1:10,000 epinephrine in 99 mL of NS
Mix 10 mL of 1:10,000 epinephrine in 1 mL of NS
Mix 1 mL of 1:1,000 epinephrine in 9 mL of NS
Mix 1 mL of 1:10,000 epinephrine in 9 mL of NS
questions.explanation: One millilitre of cardiac epinephrine 1:10,000 diluted in 9 mL of normal saline yields 10 mL of 0.001 mg/mL (1:100,000), which is injected subcutaneously for bleeding refractory to direct pressure and hemostatic gauze.

questions.title: General Trauma Care
questions.stem: What pediatric maximum does 7.04 set for subcutaneous epinephrine 0.001 mg/mL used for refractory bleeding?
questions.explanation: The pediatric ceiling is 1 mL/kg of the 0.001 mg/mL concentration, which works out to 10 mcg/kg of epinephrine.

questions.title: General Trauma Care
questions.stem: When does 7.04 direct tranexamic acid be given relative to blood products?
options: Only when blood products are unavailable
After blood administration, once life threats are addressed
Simultaneously with the first unit of blood
Before any blood product is given
questions.explanation: TXA follows blood administration where blood is available, and comes only after all other life threats have been addressed — it is never the reason a more urgent intervention waits.

questions.title: General Trauma Care
questions.stem: What does 7.04 direct a crew to do after following another trauma guideline?
options: Return to 7.04 for continued evaluation and management
Repeat the primary survey only on arrival at the facility
Contact on-line medical control before further treatment
Document the deviation in the patient care record
questions.explanation: 7.04 is the base guideline that every other trauma guideline assumes has been started, and the crew returns to it for ongoing evaluation and management after any excursion.

questions.title: General Trauma Care
questions.stem: What does 7.04 direct regarding IVs and lower priority treatments at a trauma scene?
options: Start them once airborne rather than delaying transport
Establish two large-bore IVs before moving the patient
Complete them before the patient is loaded
Defer them entirely until arrival at the receiving facility
questions.explanation: The scene emphasis is a rapid primary survey; IVs and lower priority treatments are started once airborne when practical, because transport time is the resource that matters.

questions.title: Head Injuries
questions.stem: What ETCO2 range does 7.05 direct for a ventilated patient with a head injury?
questions.explanation: The target is 35 to 40 mmHg for all known or suspected head injuries, including suspected herniation; the PEARLS note that hyperventilating to lower goals has not been shown to improve outcomes.

questions.title: Head Injuries
questions.stem: What does 7.05 suggest when ventilating an adult head-injured patient with a bag-valve mask?
options: Ventilate at a rate of 20 breaths per minute
Hyperventilate to an ETCO2 of 30 mmHg
Consider a pediatric bag to prevent hyperventilation
Use a two-person technique with an oral airway
questions.explanation: A smaller bag makes it physically harder to over-ventilate, and hyperventilation is one of the three 'H-Bombs' the guideline sets out to prevent.

questions.title: Head Injuries
questions.stem: Which three conditions does 7.05 call the 'H-Bombs' in head injury management?
questions.explanation: Each of hypoxia, hyperventilation and hypotension is independently associated with increased mortality in head injury, which is why the guideline frames preventing them as a single priority.

questions.title: Head Injuries
questions.stem: To what systolic blood pressure does 7.05 direct fluid and blood resuscitation in an ADULT with a traumatic head injury?
questions.explanation: Maintaining cerebral blood flow in an adult head injury means an SBP above 110, higher than the usual permissive targets, with vasopressors added only if the pressure is unresponsive to fluid and blood.

questions.title: Head Injuries
questions.stem: What systolic blood pressure target does 7.05 set for a PEDIATRIC head injury patient?
questions.explanation: The pediatric target is age-adjusted at 90 plus twice the age in years — deliberately above the usual pediatric hypotension formula, to protect cerebral perfusion.

questions.title: Head Injuries
questions.stem: What is the adult hypertonic saline dose for signs of herniation under 7.05?
questions.explanation: Adults get 250 mL of 3% hypertonic saline over 15 minutes, repeatable once PRN. The 5 mL/kg figure is the pediatric dose.

questions.title: Head Injuries
questions.stem: What is the pediatric hypertonic saline dose and maximum for signs of herniation under 7.05?
questions.explanation: Children get 5 mL/kg of 3% over 15 minutes capped at the 250 mL adult dose, and it may be repeated once PRN.

questions.title: Head Injuries
questions.stem: What is the mannitol dose for signs of herniation under 7.05?
questions.explanation: Mannitol is dosed at 0.5 to 1 gram/kg over 15 minutes for both adults and children, and must be given through a filter.

questions.title: Head Injuries
questions.stem: When does 7.05 direct mannitol be used rather than hypertonic saline for herniation?
options: As the first-line agent in all pediatric patients
When hypertonic saline is unavailable or ineffective
When the patient is hypotensive despite blood
When the serum sodium is below 144 mEq/L
questions.explanation: Hypertonic saline is first choice and mannitol is the fallback. Only one of the two is given, and mannitol must be obtained from the sending facility since it is not carried.

questions.title: Head Injuries
questions.stem: What piece of equipment does 7.05 require for mannitol administration?
questions.explanation: Mannitol can crystallise, so a filter is mandatory for administration.

questions.title: Head Injuries
questions.stem: What does 7.05 describe as the hallmark sign of herniation?
questions.explanation: A unilateral dilated pupil is the hallmark, progressing to bilateral and fixed as herniation worsens; posturing, Cushing reflex and contralateral hemiparesis are the other listed signs.

questions.title: Head Injuries
questions.stem: In a patient whose initial GCS was 8 or less, what GCS change does 7.05 treat as a sign of rising intracranial pressure?
options: A decrease of more than four points
A decrease of more than two points
A decrease of more than one point
questions.explanation: Where the initial GCS is already 8 or below, a fall of more than two points is listed among the signs of increased intracranial pressure and herniation.

questions.title: Head Injuries
questions.stem: Which triad does 7.05 describe as the Cushing reflex?
questions.explanation: Cushing reflex — hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respirations or apnea — is a late sign of raised intracranial pressure and herniation, not a reason to treat the blood pressure.

questions.title: Head Injuries
questions.stem: What goal serum sodium does 7.05 set for a head-injured patient?
questions.explanation: The goal is 144 to 155 mEq/L. At or above 155, repeat hypertonic saline is avoided unless hyperventilation, 30 degree head elevation and mannitol have all failed to control herniation.

questions.title: Head Injuries
questions.stem: What cerebral perfusion pressure goal does 7.05 set for adults?
questions.explanation: CPP is MAP minus ICP; adults are kept at 60 to 70 mmHg, 6 to 17 year olds at 50 to 60, and children 5 and under at 40 to 50.

questions.title: Head Injuries
questions.stem: A patient with penetrating head trauma is hypotensive with no obvious hemorrhage. What does 7.05 direct?
questions.explanation: Hypotension after penetrating head trauma is usually medullary failure rather than blood loss, so blood is withheld unless there is obvious hemorrhage to explain it.
